meta.from_author_story: A logistics client sent us 40,000 scanned bills of lading across 11 layouts. Our first pass read 62% cleanly. The failures were almost all one carrier's carbon-copy forms, and the fix was not a better model — it was a ₹4,000 scanner setting.

content.text: Manual keying of 40,000 invoices a year cost 2.3 FTE; the automated pipeline runs on 0.4 FTE of exception handling.
Document AI read 91% of invoices cleanly on day one; the remaining 9% were three vendor layouts, fixed with templates, not models.
Cycle time fell from 6.1 days to 1.6 days; the 74% figure is measured at the ninety-day mark, not the demo.
Total spend was ₹18.4 lakh including licences; payback landed in month seven.
Every automation vendor has a slide with a 90% number on it. This is the story of what the number looked like on a real accounts-payable desk in Bhiwandi, with the parts that went wrong left in.

The client is a mid-sized freight forwarder handling around 3,300 supplier invoices a month. Before the project, four people keyed those invoices into Tally by hand, matched them against purchase orders in a spreadsheet, and chased approvals over WhatsApp. The process was not broken. It was just
slow in a way nobody had measured

content.text: Six stages, two of which involve a person. The confidence gate is the part most teams skip and the part that made this work: anything the model is unsure about goes to a human before it touches the ledger, so the accounts head never had to un-trust the system.

attrs.title: How the confidence gate is set up

content.title: Log every extraction with its confidence score

body.text: Document AI returns a per-field confidence. Store all of them, not just the failures — you need the distribution to pick a threshold.

content.title: Pick the threshold from the data, not from a default

body.text: We plotted a week of scores. 0.85 caught 96% of the wrong reads while sending only 11% of invoices to a human. The vendor default of 0.7 would have let through 3× as many errors.

content.title: Route low-confidence items to a queue with the image beside the fields

body.text: The reviewer sees the scan and the extracted values side by side and corrects only the flagged field. Average handling time: 40 seconds.

content.text: The thing I did not expect was trusting it. The queue shows me exactly what it was unsure about, so I stopped checking the ones it was sure about after the second week.
Week 1–2: shadow mode. The pipeline ran beside the manual process; nothing it produced was posted.
Week 3–6: assisted mode. Humans approved every bot posting from the queue.
Week 7 onward: exception mode. Only low-confidence items reach a person.

attrs.html: This paragraph was migrated from the old article as-is. It is allowed bold and a link, and anything else is stripped:

content.question: Does this need UiPath, or does OpenBots do the whole job?

answer.text: OpenBots ran the entire posting and matching flow here. UiPath was evaluated and would have added roughly ₹4.2 lakh per bot per year in licences for the same work. The document-AI step is a separate service either platform can call.

content.question: How long did the build take?

answer.text: Eleven weeks from kickoff to exception mode, including two weeks of shadow running. The build itself was about six weeks; the rest was the confidence threshold, vendor scanner fixes and approver training.

content.question: What happens when a vendor changes their invoice layout?

answer.text: The confidence gate catches it. New layouts score low, go to a human, and the corrections feed a template for that vendor. In ninety days this happened four times and never reached the ledger uncorrected.

No single number is typical. This client had a long approval chase and a spreadsheet matching step, both of which vanished. A firm that already had an ERP with PO matching would see less on cycle time and more on keying hours.
The client does, in their own repository, with the runbook. That is standard on every build we do — one process, one price, one date, and the code is yours.
